claims.text: The Munich Residenz is the former royal palace and seat of government of the Wittelsbach monarchs of Bavaria, and stands today as the largest city palace in Germany.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The first buildings on this site were erected in 1385, financed by the citizens of Munich as a sanction for their failed uprising against the ruling dukes.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The fortress was originally built because the Dukes wanted a secure shelter to protect themselves from rebellious city dwellers and warlike relatives.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The Gothic foundation walls and the basement vaults of the old castle are the oldest surviving parts of the palace today.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: Over four centuries, the palace complex continually expanded, eventually replacing an entire former city quarter that included a monastery, barracks, houses, and gardens.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The sprawling complex now consists of three main parts, contains ten courtyards, and displays 130 rooms.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The palace's architecture blends elements from the late Renaissance, Baroque, Rococo, and Neo-Classical periods.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The Residenz Museum features the Antiquarium, a grand barrel-vaulted banqueting hall.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The Treasury holds a vast collection of ecclesiastical and secular artifacts, including the royal crowns, orb, and sceptre of the Bavarian monarchs.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: A wing of the palace known as the Festsaalbau houses the Cuvilliés Theatre and the Herkulessaal, the primary concert venue for the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The neo-classical Königsbau wing was added in the 19th century and contains the royal apartments and the Halls of Battles.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The palace was bombed during the Second World War but was painstakingly rebuilt in the post-war decades.
claims.subject: self
